issues.legal_issue: A special procedure for recovering public financial assistance as land-revenue arrears does not violate equality when the classification has a rational connection to the procedure’s purpose.
material_facts: The government advanced a loan to support the establishment of an industry, on terms that included repayment by instalments and interest below ordinary commercial lending rates.
The borrower agreed that sums due could be recovered as land-revenue arrears and later defaulted on repayment.
The government sought to use the special recovery procedure, while retaining the option of bringing a civil suit.
issues.conclusion: The classification permitting expedited recovery of qualifying public advances was reasonable and rationally related to the purpose of recovering public funds promptly; it did not violate Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits classification where it rests on a reasonable basis and has a rational relation to the law’s object. The object here was to enable prompt recovery of loans advanced by the State or the Uttar Pradesh Financial Corporation for public-development purposes, so funds could be advanced to others rather than remain tied up during ordinary civil litigation. The Court relied on Shri Manna Lal v. Collector of Jhalawar, Lachhman Das on behalf of Firm Tilak Ram Bux v. State of Punjab, and Maganlal Chhagganlal (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay; it noted that Northern India Caterers Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Punjab had been overruled. The relevant provisions were Section 3 of the Public Moneys (Recovery of Dues) Act, 1965, including Section 3(1)(c), and Sections 279 and 281 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of express statutory criteria governing when an authorized officer uses a special recovery procedure does not, by itself, make the procedure arbitrarily discriminatory when the statute’s purpose and operation guide the officer.
material_facts: The borrower argued that the statute gave the government a choice between a civil suit and the more onerous special recovery procedure without stating when the latter could be used.
The statute’s stated purpose was to provide a speedier means of recovering qualifying public dues.
The special procedure required an authorized officer to certify the sum due to the Collector, who would then proceed to recover that stated amount.
The borrower had agreed to the special recovery method and had defaulted.
issues.conclusion: The lack of express guidelines did not make the recovery procedure arbitrary or discriminatory; the statute’s purpose supplied sufficient guidance, and the officer was expected ordinarily to use the speedier procedure.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the absence of express guidelines is not sufficient, in the circumstances, to establish arbitrary power or hostile discrimination where the statutory purpose itself guides the authorized officer. It relied on Maganlal Chhagganlal (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay, which treated a statutory purpose of speedier recovery as sufficient guidance, as well as Shri Manna Lal v. Collector of Jhalawar and Lachhman Das on behalf of Firm Tilak Ram Bux v. State of Punjab. The applicable provision was Section 3 of the Public Moneys (Recovery of Dues) Act, 1965, under which an authorized officer certifies the sum due and the Collector proceeds to recover it.
